Title: Toward Real-World Adoption of Portrait Relighting via Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion
Text:
Toward Real-World Adoption of Portrait
Relighting via Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion
Qian Huang, Mayoore Selvarasa Jaiswal, Zhen Zhong, Rochelle Pereira, and
Jianyuan Min
NVIDIA
{qianh, mjaiswal, zhenz, rpereira, jmin}@nvidia.com
Abstract. The real-world adoption of portrait relighting is hindered
by dataset domain gaps, camera sensitivity, and computational costs.
We address these challenges with Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion, a
paradigm that fuses the specialized strengths of synthetic, One-Light-
at-A-Time (OLAT), and real-world datasets into a compact model. Our
approach features specialized prior models hardened by domain-aware
adaptation, followed by augmented knowledge distillation into a lightweight
student model with multi-domain expertise. Our method demonstrates a
6× to 240× inference speedup while maintaining state-of-the-art (SOTA)
visual quality in the experiments. Additionally, we construct a massive,
high-fidelity synthetic dataset with diverse ground-truth intrinsics to
support our training pipeline.
Keywords: Portrait Relighting · Knowledge Distillation · Domain
Adaptation
1
Introduction
Video portrait relighting, which aims to re-illuminate subjects to match target
High Dynamic Range Images (HDRI), has become an active area in academia
and industry, driven by the escalating demand spanning from daily life like im-
mersive telepresence and live streaming, to professional media production like
cinematic visual effects. For real-world deployment, a relighting algorithm is
required to be versatile and faithful to handle unconstrained subjects and en-
vironmental lighting; robust to distinct cameras; and lightweight for real-time
execution with temporal stability.
The learning-based approaches have set new standards for visual quality. Re-
garding the rendering process, the research landscape diverges into physically-
based rendering and pure neural rendering. The former integrate explicit re-
flectance models (e.g., Phong or Cook-Torrance BRDFs) in their architectures,
while the latter is model-free, utilizing pure networks to learn relighting physics.
Diffusion-based generative models in the pure neural category have rapidly risen
to prominence [7, 22] due to their superb ability of synthesizing photorealistic

ments. Because diffusion models are stochastic denoisers in essence, they are
prone to corrupt fine-grained facial features and skin textures, leading to un-
intended identity shifts and hallucinated semantics [19]. Furthermore, diffusion

Physically-based neural rendering methods [15, 24, 35] on the other hand
ensure rigorous light transport process and excel at identity preservation. Yet,
these methods are brittle in the wild due to data domain gap. The absence of
paired in-the-wild captures with ground-truth intrinsic components forces the
algorithms to rely on data from controlled environments (e.g., light stage or
synthetic data). Consequently, these models exhibit poor extrapolation to diverse
environmental lighting and real-world camera configurations, deteriorating when
confronted with the sensor noise, lens glare, and motion blur inherent to real
environments. To compensate, they frequently employ heavy architectures that
move away from low-latency on consumer hardware.


Toward Real-World Adoption of Portrait Relighting
3
To overcome these challenges, we introduce Hybrid Domain Knowledge
Fusion. Rather than attempting to let a single model extrapolate from ho-
mogeneous or mainly homogeneous data, we decouple the learning process into
two steps. First, we develop specialized prior models that master specific domain
knowledge of synthetic data, One-Light-at-A-Time (OLAT) data, and unlabelled
real data. To dissolve the domain gaps, we introduce targeted augmentations
to prior models against camera artifacts, novel albedo consistency constraints
against ambient lighting, and a 2D Layer Normalization (LN) that stabilizes
cross-domain statistics. Second, we fuse this multi-domain expertise into a single,
lightweight student network via augmented knowledge distillation. This distilla-
tion framework goes beyond model compression. It leverages massive real data to
generate domain-routed rich pseudo ground truth regarding the characteristics
of each prior, which effectively absorbs domain knowledge. Instead of relying on
the raw outputs of the prior models, it applies asymmetric augmentation only
to the input of the student model but not the prior model, for the purpose of
going even beyond the robustness of prior models.
In summary, our primary contributions are:
– We propose Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion, a novel training paradigm
that bridges the distinct domain gap through prior model training with do-
main adaptation and augmented knowledge distillation. This results in a
realistic, robust and compact model that is ready for real-world adoption.
– We present the fastest video portrait relighting model, achieving real-time
performance on consumer-grade edge hardware (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 2060)
without compromising visual quality.
– We construct a massive, high-fidelity synthetic portrait relighting dataset
powered by NVIDIA Omniverse and Digital Human Technology, with rich
demographic diversity and explicit intrinsic components, supporting our
physically-based rendering pipeline.
2
Related Work
2.1
Deep Learning for Portrait Relighting
Learning-based relighting can be classified into pure neural rendering and physically-
based rendering. Pure neural approaches, particularly diffusion models, excel at
synthesizing complex illumination and light scattering [7, 12, 22, 37]. However,
their sequential denoising mechanism poses challenges for real-world applications
due to heavy computation and temporal inconsistency [10, 14]. Furthermore,
their stochastic nature frequently hallucinates semantic features [19], causing
unintended identity shifts that preclude their use in fidelity-sensitive scenarios.
In comparison, physically-based rendering approaches explicitly model light
transport by decomposing portraits into intrinsic components (e.g., albedo, nor-
mal) and applying established reflectance models [15, 24, 35]. This paradigm
guarantees photometric linearity and excels at identity preservation. However,
achieving high-fidelity intrinsic decomposition requires supervision from light

stage captures or synthetic data. While accurate within these controlled distri-
butions, these models suffer from a domain gap when extrapolated to highly
diverse, unconstrained real-world captures.
To meet the strict latency requirements of real-time applications, recent ar-
chitectures employ simplified diffuse shading [20], low-order Spherical Harmon-
ics [6], or lightweight encoder-decoder networks that heavily compress physical
priors [28, 36]. While elegantly optimized for rapid inference, simplifying these
rendering equations fundamentally compromises high-frequency lighting effects
like specularities. Furthermore, the resulting acceleration is often still insufficient
to guarantee stable, real-time performance on entry-level consumer hardware.
2.2
Domain Adaptation and Knowledge Distillation
To overcome computational bottlenecks without sacrificing visual fidelity, re-
cent works have adapted Knowledge Distillation (KD) [13] to neural render-
ing [3,9] and lighting prior extraction [4]. However, applying generalized KD to
physically-based portrait relighting presents a unique structural challenge: the
massive domain gap between pristine synthetic training data and degraded real-
world inference captures. Standard KD objectives become poorly conditioned
when forcing a student network to map noisy, out-of-distribution inputs directly
to representations learned exclusively from clean data, resulting in degraded
relighting accuracy.
To address this, we propose the first multi-teacher knowledge distillation
framework uniquely designed to fuse heterogeneous data domains for physically-
based relighting. By routing distillation through multiple domain-specific teach-
ers and applying asymmetric linear-radiance augmentations, our approach trans-
fers the precise physical accuracy of synthetic experts while explicitly hardening
the student network against unconstrained real-world optical degradations.
3
Method
We introduce Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion, a paradigm that bridges the
domain gap between isolated training datasets and unconstrained real-world de-
ployment. The pipeline consists of two phases: training three specialized, cross-
domain-aware prior models (Pphys, Prefl, Preal), and distilling their fused ex-
pertise into a compact, real-time student model S.
3.1
Prior Models
To initiate the fusion process, we develop three specialized prior models (Pphys,
Prefl, Preal) to extract and refine high-level knowledge bases. The Physics Prior
(Pphys) focuses on learning the fundamental physics of light-surface interaction
and intrinsic components from high-fidelity synthetic data. The Reflectance Prior
(Prefl) focuses on learning the subsurface scattering and specularity of human

3.2
Domain Adaptation Mechanisms
Forward Models and Augmentations. To bridge the discrepancy between
perfectly clean synthetic/OLAT renderings and recorded media from real imag-
ing devices, we construct forward models including glare, noise and motion that
are important to the relighting problem, and design standard data augmenta-
tions accordingly. By enforcing these augmentation mechanisms during the prior
training phase, we force the priors to develop robustness of relighting to imaging
devices, configurations, and environments.
The composite forward model in the raw space is formulated as:

Glare Augmentation. Glare is from the scattering of light within a lens assembly,
prominent when the lens points at high-intensity sources (e.g., the sun or a bright
lamp). The glare is modelled as an additive process to a clean image [33] via 2D
convolution [2,29] between the light source image L and point spread function
K.
  \ m athbf {G} = \mathbf {L} \circledast \mathbf {K} 
(2)
We simulate light sources L as randomized geometric primitives with random size
and color. We randomly sample between a Moffat PSF, K(r) ∝(1 + r2/σ2)−β
and an exponential PSF, K(r) ∝exp(−rβ/σ2).
Noise Augmentation. We adapt the noise-free synthetic data to mimic inputs
from everyday cameras by introducing realistic noise NGAN. We create a noise
dataset and train a generative network to produce noise for our augmentation.
The dataset was built on a set of sequences of static scenes, acquired with differ-
ent Logitech cameras, spatially registered to guarantee pixel accuracy, and tem-
porally filtered to isolate the temporal noise component in sets of 8 × 8 patches.
We use these additive noise patches to train a GAN [11] using UNet [27] to
generate more noise samples to augment the training data. We apply identical
noise profiles to both the input and the target ground truth during training.
This forces the prior models to remain robust to noise rather than attempting
to perform denoising.
Motion Blur and Spatial Augmentations. To account for subject movement and
camera shake, we incorporate a motion blur stage. The forward model of the
motion blur is also known as convolution. We apply a 1D motion kernel Bk,θ
with pixel length k and orientation θ. This is combined with a suite of spatial
augmentations, including random scaling, rotation and cropping, to improve the
model’s translation and scale invariance.
Albedo Consistency Constraints. We enforce two albedo consistency losses
to ensure the model maintains lighting-invariant surface properties and remains
independent of external illumination on unlabelled real-world data.
We define f as our relighting model, fA as the albedo estimation function,
and E as the HDRI. Given a foreground input image I and two distinct HDRIs
E1 and E2 randomly sampled from database, we require the network to predict
identical albedo maps regardless of the requested lighting:
  \m a thcal {L }_{e n v} = \|  f_A[f(\mathbf {I}, \mathbf {E_1})] - f_A[f(\mathbf {I}, \mathbf {E_2})] \|_1 
(3)
This self-consistency forces the model to mathematically decouple intrinsic re-
flectance from light transport, ensuring the subject’s identity and skin properties
remain stable.
To further isolate albedo from photometric fluctuations from the environment
(e.g., brightness and contrast changes), we enforce ambient consistency:
  \m a thcal  {L} _ {amb} =  \| f_A[\mathcal {T}(\mathbf {I})] - f_A(\mathbf {I}) \|_1\,, 
(4)

where T denotes a global brightness or contrast transformation. By requiring
the albedo to remain constant under varying input intensities, we guarantee
algorithmic robustness across different camera sensors.
The overall albedo consistency loss is formulated as:
  \mathc a l {L}_{c o nsist} = \lambda _{env} \mathcal {L}_{env} + \lambda _{amb} \mathcal {L}_{amb}

Domain-Aware Layer Normalization. To mitigate the severe statistical
variance encountered when fusing synthetic, OLAT, and real-world datasets,
we adopt 2D layer normalization [21] across the network. Normalizing indepen-
dently across the spatial and channel dimensions for each instance stabilizes
cross-domain feature distributions and prevents statistical mismatch during in-
ference.
3.3
Augmented Knowledge Distillation
The multi-domain expertise of the prior models is distilled into a single, highly
efficient student network S.
Architectural Compression. We systematically compress S by reducing
the channel capacity of the normal, albedo, shading, and rendering modules by
a factor of four. Because supervised student training resolves the severe cross-
domain batch variance handled during prior training, we adopt BN that favors
hardware acceleration, except for albedo modules. These modifications drasti-
cally reduce inference latency.
Domain-Routed Pseudo-Ground Truth Supervision. To fuse the spe-
cialized capabilities of the prior models, subsets of the training data are explic-
itly routed to the prior model best suited for that specific domain. The selected
teacher generates high-fidelity pseudo-ground truths of normals, albedos, diffuse
and specular weights, light maps, and the final rendered output.
Asymmetric Augmentation. To let the student model surpass the in-the-
wild robustness of its teachers, the augmentation is performed asymmetrically
during distillation. Specifically, the prior models receive the original (unaug-
mented) input to generate clean pseudo-labels, while the student model is aug-
mented using the degradations from Sec. 3.2 plus contrast, brightness, and am-
bient color augmentation. This approach effectively allows our model to learn
representations that are robust to artifacts.
3.4
Network Architecture and Training Details
Prior Models. Our prior models adopt the Phong-based network architec-
ture [35], which decomposes the foreground into surface normal and diffuse
albedo. The predicted normal is used to generate a diffuse light map and multi-
ple specular light maps from pre-convolved environment maps [23]. A rendering
network predicts per-pixel weights to fuse these light maps and estimates an ad-
ditive residual for the final relit image. The original framework has three training

stages: fully supervised pretraining on a virtual light stage dataset; unsupervised
syn2real adaptation to refine the albedo with residual layers using real images
and self-supervised lighting consistency losses; and temporal refinement through
residual layers using optical flow. These networks are implemented using a UNet
architecture. We replace the standard BN with 2D LN across all networks to en-
sure statistical stability across domains. We also halve the channel capacity and
residual block counts of [35] and employ a multi-resolution strategy: the normal
network operates at 512 × 512 while all other modules process at 768 × 768. We
empirically observe that these modifications provide a 4× efficiency boost while
maintaining comparable visual fidelity.
All prior models are trained using the Adam [16] optimizer with 0.0001 learn-
ing rate with 8 batch on 8 NVIDIA A100 GPUs. Pphys is trained from scratch
on our synthetic dataset for 100k iterations, optimized via L1, perceptual, and
GAN losses applied to the predicted surface normals, diffuse albedo, and final
RGB output, following the configurations in [24]. It is subsequently fine-tuned
on our real data for an additional 50k iterations, following [35]. This unsuper-
vised phase minimizes the composite loss L = Lconsist + λT
adapLadap, where
Ladap = [LColat, LCrela, Lsim, LId, LG]T enforces lighting consistency, relative
lighting consistency, perceptual similarity, and identity preservation. The weights
are empirically set to λenv = 25 and λamb = 500, and λadap = [10, 50, 10, 1, 1]T
corresponding to the respective losses in Ladap.
Prefl is trained jointly on our synthetic and OLAT datasets for 100k it-
erations. Glare augmentation is applied with probability p = 0.5. The specific
augmentation parameters are uniformly sampled within the given range: the PSF
standard deviation σ ∈[50, 200] pixels, shape β ∈[1.0, 3.0], and glare intensity
α ∈[1.0, 3.0]. Motion blur k ∈[15, 25] pixels and θ ∈[0, 2π] radians, along with
spatial augmentations (resize, rotation, crop) via Albumentations [5] are applied
with p = 0.5 probability.
Preal is initialized from the Prefl checkpoint and fine-tuned on our real data.
This phase utilizes the same unsupervised configuration used in Pphys, except
that λsim and λId are doubled to 2 to enforce strict identity fidelity.
Distilled Student Model. The compressed student network S is trained for
125k iterations at 768×768 resolution. Optimization utilizes the Adam optimizer
with a batch size 2 per GPU across 16 NVIDIA A100 GPUs and increased
learning rate of 0.0002.
Distillation relies on an explicit, domain-routed batch composition mapping
inputs to specific teachers: 75% of each batch (60% curated images, 15% HD-
VILA frames) is supervised by Preal; 10% (OLAT data) is supervised by Prefl;
and the remaining 15% (a residual pool isolating complex-identity subjects) is
supervised by Pphys.
During the asymmetric augmentation phase, the student’s inputs are de-
graded with p = 0.5 probability. The overall distillation objective comprises the
same supervised losses as in Pphys, augmented with a differentiable color his-
togram loss [1, 26] to align global color and illumination distributions against

4
Datasets
To support the Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion paradigm, we construct a
massive training database comprising over 640k synthetic renders, 200k OLAT
renders, and 650k unlabelled real-world image and video sequences.
4.1
Synthetic Dataset
One of our contributions is a high-fidelity, large-scale dataset leveraging NVIDIA
Omniverse and Digital Human Technology. To prevent dataset bias and ensure
broad generalization across populations, we construct 800 avatars, 300 from Dig-
ital Human Generator API and 500 from RenderPeople1, with unique identities,
grooming, clothing and accessories. We further introduce skin tone and texture
perturbations to the digital human avatars.
Subjects are illuminated under over 2100 HDRIs with randomized rotations
to simulate diverse illumination. This includes 1608 real-world environments ac-
quired from various databases, 471 synthetically generated HDRs with enhanced
directional lighting, and 44 HDRs covering varied scenery and lighting scenarios.
The data generation pipeline renders subjects using diversified camera loca-
tion and poses, and exports perfectly pixel-aligned 3840 × 2160 RGB render-
ings, alpha matting, diffuse albedos, and surface normals for over 340k samples
through Omniverse Replicator extension as ground truth. Unlike prior work that
relies on slower path tracers [35], our pipeline utilizes the NVIDIA RTX Real-
Time engine. By explicitly enabling Subsurface Scattering and Deep Learning
Anti-Aliasing, we simulate the complex light transport and scattering properties
of human skin while maintaining extreme computational efficiency.
To expand diversity, we supplement these renderings with an additional 300k
samples rendered from TripleGanger scans at 512 × 512.
4.2
OLAT Dataset
We utilize raw light stage [8] captures comprising 320 diverse subjects, each
recorded with 2 facial expressions using 7 frontal cameras and 164 LEDs. Train-
ing pairs are synthesized via linear superposition of the OLAT captures [8]
weighted by randomly rotated HDR environment maps.
Explicit intrinsic supervision is extracted directly from the captures: surface
normals are derived via photometric stereo [32], and diffuse albedos are approx-
imated using images captured under flat omnidirectional lighting [24]. We adopt
NVIDIA Maxine SDK2 to extract the foreground image (same for real dataset).
We hold out 32 identities to form our quantitative evaluation test set.

4.3
Real Dataset
To capture the long-tail distribution of unconstrained identities, lighting, and
imaging devices, we curate 22k real images from online videos and proprietary
collections, spanning low-end webcams to professional cameras.
We subsample 650k clips from two benchmarks, TalkingHead-1kH [30] and
HD-VILA [34], to form our video dataset. They provide continuous motion,
natural pose variations, and dynamic lighting changes for the student model to
achieve robust video relighting. The evaluation set utilizes held-out frames from
online videos and internal captures.
5
Experiments and Results
We evaluate our method along three axes: visual quality, computational effi-
ciency, and design choices. For visual quality, we conduct quantitative and quali-
tative assessments on held-out OLAT data (Sec. 4.2) with pixel-accurate ground
truth and on unconstrained in-the-wild portraits under diverse HDR lighting.
For efficiency, we benchmark inference latency against competing methods un-
der matched hardware conditions. Finally, we perform ablation studies to isolate
the contribution of each key component.
Evaluation Metrics. Following established protocols [22, 24, 35], we re-
port Mean Squared Error (MSE), Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR), Struc-
tural Similarity (SSIM) [31], and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity
(LPIPS) [38]. All metrics are computed on the foreground region using pre-
computed segmentation masks.
Baselines. We compare against six recent portrait relighting methods: LU-
MOS [35], DiffusionRenderer [17], UniRelight [12], IC-Light [37], SwitchLight
v3 [15], and 3D-Aware Relighting [6]. For SwitchLight we use their released por-
tal3; all other methods use publicly available codebases. 3D-Aware Relighting
operates on tightly cropped faces and does not relight the full upper body; it is
therefore included in qualitative comparisons but excluded from the quantitative
benchmark.
5.1
Visual Quality
OLAT Benchmark. We evaluate on a held-out test set of 32 identities from the
light stage captures described in Sec. 4.2. Ground-truth relit images are synthe-
sized by linearly superimposing per-light OLAT frames weighted by target in-
the-wild HDR environment maps, following the reflectance field formulation [8].
Because this superposition is physically grounded, the resulting targets serve as
pixel-accurate references for all metrics.
Qualitatively (Figure 3), our relit outputs most closely match the ground
truth in brightness, light direction, and skin tone. Quantitatively (Table 1), our
method achieves the best MSE, PSNR, and SSIM, and remains competitive in

Relighting Fidelity. Beyond pixel-level metrics, faithful relighting must
preserve the subject’s identity–skin tone, facial features, and material appearance–
while coherently adopting the target illumination. We evaluate this on a diverse
set of portraits captured with cameras of varying quality, relit under a com-
mon target HDR environment (Figure 4). Our method maintains the highest fi-
delity to the original subject, producing accurate skin tones and natural shadow
placement under the new lighting. In contrast, DiffusionRenderer [17] introduces
excessive specularity that alters facial appearance, and SwitchLight v3 [15] over-
smooths skin and hair texture, yielding a synthetic, computer-generated look.
Across all baselines, we observe recurring failure modes—residual ambient light-
ing, global color shifts, or loss of fine detail—that degrade identity consistency
relative to our method.

6
Conclusion
We presented Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion, a training paradigm that ad-
dresses three core barriers to real-world portrait relighting: the domain gap be-
tween controlled training data and unconstrained deployment, sensitivity to di-
verse imaging devices, and prohibitive computational cost. Our approach devel-
ops three specialized prior models—physics, reflectance, and realism—each mas-
tering a complementary data domain through targeted augmentations, albedo
consistency constraints, and domain-aware normalization. These priors are then
fused into a single compact student network via augmented knowledge distil-
lation, which combines domain-routed pseudo-ground truth supervision with
asymmetric augmentation to produce a model that is simultaneously accurate,
robust, and fast.
Experiments demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art relight-
ing quality on OLAT benchmarks while delivering 6× to 240× speedups over
existing approaches, reaching 84 fps on an entry-level RTX 2060 and exceeding
500 fps on an RTX 4090 at 512 × 512 resolution. We additionally construct a
large-scale, high-fidelity synthetic dataset with pixel-aligned ground-truth in-
trinsic components used in our training pipeline.

C
Additional Details on the Synthetic Dataset
Our dataset is rendered utilizing the NVIDIA Omniverse Replicator extension.
To ensure the model learns a highly generalized representation, the dataset com-
prises an expansive manifold of identities. As visualized in Figure 13, our data
generation strategy explicitly randomizes multiple core attributes in the real-
world relighting task to maximize structural and photometric diversity:
– Identity and Skin Tone: The dataset spans a comprehensive spectrum of ages,
facial structures, and skin reflectance properties. To mitigate demographic
bias, procedural shader-level perturbations are applied during generation,
randomly sampling melanin density and subsurface redness parameters.
– Grooming and Accessories: Subjects are rendered with a wide variety of hair
and beard styles. We also introduce accessories that are common in daily
life, such as varying styles of headsets and eyeglasses.
– Attire and Textiles: We simulate clothing with diverse patterns and graphics
by procedurally mapping textures onto the UV coordinates of the garment
meshes. Specifically, we sample from a collection of 2,000 images across 8
categories sourced from OpenClipArt5. These patterns act as alpha masks
to modulate the diffuse albedo with randomized color palettes.
– Poses and Illumination: Subjects are rendered across varying body poses
from frontal to profiles to ensure rotation-invariant intrinsic estimation.

Abstract: The real-world adoption of portrait relighting is hindered by dataset domain gaps, camera sensitivity, and computational costs. We address these challenges with Hybrid Domain Knowledge Fusion, a paradigm that fuses the specialized strengths of synthetic, One-Light- at-A-Time (OLAT), and real-world datasets into a compact model. Our approach features specialized prior models hardened by domain-aware adaptation, followed by augmented knowledge distillation into a lightweight student model with multi-domain expertise. Our method demonstrates a 6× to 240× inference speedup while maintaining state-of-the-art (SOTA) visual quality in the experiments. Additionally, we construct a massive, high-fidelity synthetic dataset with diverse ground-truth intrinsics to support our training pipeline.
